conservation.notes: Widespread and often common; the most commonly observed bird in the annual BirdLife Australia census. Some localised taxa of the former T. haematodus complex are more precarious, notably the Biak lorikeet (T. rosenbergii), which is threatened by habitat loss and capture for the parrot trade.

human_tolerance.notes: Frequent visitor at garden bird feeders and semitame in many suburban backyards, especially around Sydney; wild birds at campsites and in wildlife parks are so used to people that they settle on visitors' arms and heads to be hand-fed. The same tameness brings noise and fouling complaints, and fruit-orchard owners treat the species as a pest. light_max is an authored judgement.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Southern Australia: 'breeding usually occurs from late winter to early summer (August to January)'. Elsewhere in Australia breeding has been recorded in every month except March, varying region to region with food availability and climate, so this window is the sourced southern-Australian season, not a range-wide one.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Derived from the sourced breeding window and the 25-day incubation of a clutch of one to three eggs, with altricial young then carried in the nest hollow for several further weeks; fledging age was not found in an open source, so this window is a derived approximation.

vocalizations.description: The species' characteristic call: a harsh, rasping, metallic screech given constantly in flight and from flowering trees, rising and falling in pitch. Lorikeets have no true song, so the program's 'song' slot carries this screech instead.
A sudden burst of loud, harsh screeching when a bird is startled or a flock is flushed, usually immediately on take-off.

Continuous overlapping screeching and chattering of a large feeding or roosting aggregation, as described for the twice-daily noisy flock that gathers in the main area at Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary. Dawn and dusk windows are an authored judgement about when flocks move between roost and foraging.

taxonomy.note: GBIF's usage record for key 2479694 carries taxonomicStatus SYNONYM and points at acceptedKey 6170530, Trichoglossus haematodus moluccanus (a subspecies), so taxonomy.status is Synonym and taxonomy.accepted_id names that accepted trinomial. The 2019 revision that elevated the Australian birds is summarised in the Wikipedia Taxonomy section, which is why the Wikipedia article and this record both use the binomen T. moluccanus while the GBIF backbone has not yet been updated.

external.note: GBIF usage key from the GBIF backbone record; iNaturalist taxon id 980095, Wikidata id Q1809222 and NCBI taxon id 1549204 (P685) from Wikidata; ITIS TSN 714103 from the ITIS JSON service. No eBird code is recorded: none was confirmed from an open source in this work.

common_names.note: English, French ('Loriquet de Swainson') and Dutch ('Lori van de Blauwe Bergen') labels from Wikidata Q1809222; the English name is also the Wikipedia article title. German 'Regenbogenlori' is the German Wikipedia article title, used because Wikidata's German label is the scientific name.

conservation.note: Wikipedia Status section: the annual Birdlife Australia census has it as the most commonly observed bird in Australia, so BirdLife International treats it as Least Concern; the article's taxobox carries the IUCN 3.1 status LC (assessment e.T22725334A95228767), and Wikidata Q1809222 P141 is 'least concern'. The Biak lorikeet caution comes from the same section.

range.note: Wikipedia Range and habitat section: the east coast of Australia from northern Queensland south through New South Wales, then west through Victoria and South Australia, in forest, shrubland, wetlands and some artificial habitats, so native is AU. Introduced populations are the lead section's Auckland (New Zealand) and Hong Kong; the same lead lists Perth (Western Australia) and Tasmania as introductions, and the As a pest section explains that the Perth population has been self-sustaining since the 1960s and is now a declared pest there, so AU is listed under invasive_in rather than introduced. The record carries no separate introduced code for Tasmania, which is a state of AU and therefore already covered by the native code.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Powered flight is explicit. Parrots hop on branches, feeders and the ground and climb with beak and feet, but 'Climb' is not offered as a move pose by the biped_winged body plan, so only Hop and Fly are listed as locomotion modes to keep every declared mode resolvable to a pose.

traits.nest_type.note: Breeding section: nesting sites are variable and can include hollows of tall trees such as eucalypts, palm trunks or overhanging rock, and pairs sometimes nest in the same tree as other pairs or other bird species.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.116 kg falls in the Small band).

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the stated weight range, 75-157 g, from the Wikipedia Description section (116 g). AnAge independently gives an adult weight of 115.1 g, so the midpoint is not an artefact of the range.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Wikipedia Description section: 'the weight varies from 75 to 157 g'.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the stated total length range, 25-30 cm, including the tail.

traits.lifespan_y.note: AnAge gives maximum longevity 20.6 years in the wild, attributed to Australian Bird and Bat Banding Scheme banding records, with data quality 'Acceptable' and a large sample. That is a documented maximum rather than a typical value, so it is rounded down to 20 years here for the schema's 'typical lifespan' field.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Judgement, and the one number in this record with no source at all. The validator requires wingspan_m for a species with Fly locomotion, but no open-licensed wingspan measurement for T. moluccanus was found: Wikidata Q1809222 carries no wingspan (P2050) statement, and the English Wikipedia article gives length (25-30 cm) and weight (75-157 g) but no wingspan. The 45 cm figure is an authored estimate for a long-tailed parrot of 25-30 cm total length, and should be replaced with a measurement from an openly licensed Australian government, museum or university source if one is found. A reviewer should treat this as the record's weakest field, not as a measurement.

traits.diet.note: Wikipedia Diet section: lorikeets 'feed mainly on fruit, pollen, and nectar' with a papillate tongue appendage for gathering pollen and nectar, eucalyptus nectar being the key Australian source. The section gives no quantified shares, so the split is an authored judgement mapping: pollen folded into nectar (0.5) because both are taken from the same flowers with the same tongue; fruit (0.35) from Ficus, Trema and Muntingia, papaya, mango and opened fruit; and seed (0.15) from raided maize and sorghum and from the sunflower seed put out at feeders. No invertebrate component was found, so none is claimed.

traits.social.note: Breeding section: 'mostly monogamous and remain paired for long periods, if not for life', so the pair is the basic unit, but the Diet section describes large aggregations — thousands of birds gathering twice daily in a huge, noisy flock at Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary, and semitame visitors to Sydney backyards — and individual birds are then indistinguishable in a crowd, so Flock is used as the structure. The group_size bounds are an authored judgement: a lower bound of 2 for a nesting pair and an upper bound of 60 for a typical day-to-day feeding flock, well below the thousands-scale sanctuary and wild aggregations.

traits.activity_pattern.note: No explicit 'diurnal' statement, but all described activity is by day: the twice-daily 8 am and 4 pm flock at Currumbin, and feeding and flocking across the day.

traits.defense.note: Judgement: no explicit predator-response description was found. A fast, noisy flier that flushes in a screeching flock and nests in tree hollows, consistent with other parrot records in this repository.

traits.wariness.note: Set very low from the Diet section: 'wild lorikeets are so used to humans that they can be hand-fed', they settle on visitors' arms and heads at Currumbin, and semitame birds are common daily visitors in Sydney backyards. 0.15 keeps a little startle response, since feeding flocks still flush noisily when closely approached.

habitat.use.note: Judgement: predominantly arboreal, from the lead's 'rainforest, coastal bush, and woodland areas' and the use of tree hollows, with regular ground-level use at feeders, campsites and wildlife-park feeding displays.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Roosts and perches in tall trees and around the hollows it nests in; 'perch' is used as the closest available ResourceTag.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet, with the nectar resource given kind Nectarivory. Cavity nesting and perch shelter come from the Breeding and Diet sections.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Urban affinity and garden use from the Diet section (garden bird feeders, hand-feeding, semitame Sydney backyards) and the lead's 'some artificial habitats'; the nuisance and orchard-pest framing is from the As a pest section. light_max is an authored judgement for a species routinely active and feeding in lit suburban and city parks.

seasonal.strategy.note: Breeding section: breeding has been recorded in every month except March, varying region to region with food availability and climate, so the species is resident rather than migratory.

seasonal.phases.note: The breeding window is the Wikipedia Breeding section's stated southern-Australian season (late winter to early summer, August to January). The young window is derived from it plus the same section's ~25-day incubation of a one-to-three-egg clutch; the fledging age was not available from an open source, so that window is an approximation rather than a sourced date.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg, altricial juvenile and adult inferred from the sourced clutch size, ~25-day incubation by the female alone, and hollow rearing; no open source gives a juvenile duration or size, so both were left unset rather than guessed.

vocalizations.screech.note: Judgement on the call's character: the Wikipedia article calls the species 'noisy' and describes the twice-daily 'huge, noisy flock' at Currumbin, but it contains no description of the call itself and the species has no true song. The harsh in-flight screech, its context, loudness and the use of the behavior program's 'song' slot are therefore authored; the program's slot name is not a claim that the species sings.

vocalizations.alarm_screech.note: Judgement: a startled flush alarm call is inferred from the species' social flocking and habit of feeding in exposed trees near people, both described in the Diet section; no open source characterises the alarm call specifically.

vocalizations.flock_chatter.note: Derived from the Diet section's 'huge, noisy flock' of thousands at Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary and its semitame flocking in Sydney backyards; the dawn/dusk time windows are an authored judgement about when flocks move between roost and foraging, and the call is modelled on contact calling rather than on a transcribed sound.

look.note: Colours from the Wikipedia Description section: 'The head is deep blue with a greenish-yellow nuchal collar, and the rest of the upper parts (wings, back, and tail) are green. The chest is orange/yellow. The belly is deep blue, and the thighs and rump are green. In flight, a yellow wing-bar contrasts clearly with the red underwing coverts', plus the adult's red-orange bill (black in juveniles). Mapped to the block model's five slots as body green, belly blue, breast orange (markings), bill and underwing red (accent), and a nape collar rendered in the markings slot. The greenish-yellow nuchal collar, the yellow wing-bar and the red underwing coverts cannot all be shown in five slots, and the two sexes are identical so no dimorphic part is modelled. Proportions — stocky torso, long tapered tail, large head, short legs, strong hooked bill — are authored judgement for a Trichoglossus lorikeet.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program. food_tag is nectar rather than seed because this is a nectar-and-fruit feeder with a brush-tipped tongue (see traits.diet). The program's 'song' and 'alarm' slots are filled with the screech and alarm-screech calls, since the species has no song. flee_m is reduced from the program's 6 m to 5 m for a notably tame bird that hand-feeds, and wariness is 0.15 for the same reason. nest_m1/nest_m2 are 8/12: the program's nesting branch is hard-coded to run from nest_m1 through months 4-6 to nest_m2, so it cannot express the sourced southern-Australian August-January season without changing a shared program that other species use; an August-December window is the closest in-year fit and the real season is recorded in seasonal.phases.
